claim: In most well-studied rod-shaped bacteria, peptidoglycan is primarily crosslinked by penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs).
source: In most well-studied rod-shaped bacteria, peptidoglycan is primarily crosslinked by penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field, drawing from scientific consensus about bacterial cell wall structure.

claim: In mycobacteria, crosslinks formed by L,D-transpeptidases (LDTs) are highly abundant.
source: However, in mycobacteria, crosslinks formed by L,D-transpeptidases (LDTs) are highly abundant.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on mycobacterial peptidoglycan composition.

claim: Crosslinks generated by LDTs are required for rod shape maintenance specifically at sites of aging cell wall.
source: We find that crosslinks generate by LDTs are required for rod shape maintenance specifically at sites of aging cell wall, a byproduct of polar elongation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental observations of ΔLDT cells losing rod shape at aging cell wall regions.

claim: Asymmetric polar growth leads to a non-uniform distribution of 4-3 and 3-3 crosslinks in a single cell.
source: Asymmetric polar growth leads to a non-uniform distribution of these two types of crosslinks in a single cell.
evidence: This is supported by FDAA incorporation patterns and localization studies of PBPs and LDTs shown in the figures.

claim: In the absence of LDT-mediated crosslinks, PBP-catalyzed crosslinks become more important.
source: Consequently, in the absence of LDT-mediated crosslinks, PBP-catalyzed crosslinks become more important.
evidence: This is supported by TnSeq data showing that PBPs become essential in ΔLDT cells.

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is more rapidly killed using a combination of drugs capable of PBP- and LDT- inhibition.
source: Because of this, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is more rapidly killed using a combination of drugs capable of PBP- and LDT- inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing synergistic killing with amoxicillin and meropenem combinations.

claim: Peptidoglycan consists of linear glycan strands crosslinked by short peptides to form a continuous molecular cage surrounding the plasma membrane.
source: PG consists of linear glycan strands crosslinked by short peptides to form a continuous molecular cage surrounding the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan structure.

claim: In E. coli and B. subtilis, new PG is constructed along the lateral side wall.
source: In these organisms, new PG is constructed along the lateral side wall by the concerted effort of glycosyltransferases, which connect the glycan of a new PG subunit to the existing mesh, and transpeptidases, which link peptide side chains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lateral cell wall growth in model bacteria, supported by citations.

claim: MreB positions the PG synthesis complex along the short axis of the cell so that glycan strands are inserted circumferentially in E. coli and B. subtilis.
source: An actin-like protein, MreB, positions this multi-protein complex along the short axis of the cell so that glycan strands are inserted circumferentially, creating discontinuous hoops of PG around the cell (Domínguez-Escobar et al., 2011; Garner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on MreB function.

claim: The circumferential orientation of PG creates a mechanical anisotropy that is responsible for rod shape in E. coli and B. subtilis.
source: This orientation of PG creates a mechanical anisotropy that is responsible for rod shape (Hussain et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mycobacteria do not encode MreB.
source: However, not all rod-shaped bacteria encode MreB.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial genetics.

claim: In mycobacteria, new PG is inserted at the cell poles at unequal amounts based on pole age.
source: In mycobacteria, new PG is inserted at the cell poles (at unequal amounts based on pole age), rather than along the lateral walls (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the schematic in Figure 1A and established knowledge about mycobacterial growth.

claim: Mycobacteria are missing several factors, including MreB, that are important for cell elongation.
source: Additionally, mycobacteria are missing several factors, including MreB, that are important for cell elongation (Kieser and Rubin, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In E. coli and B. subtilis, the vast majority (>90%) of peptide linkages are created by D,D-transpeptidases known as penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs).
source: Furthermore, in E. coli and B. subtilis the vast majority (>90%) of the peptide linkages are created by D,D-transpeptidases known as penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) (Pisabarro et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PBPs link the fourth amino acid of one peptide side chain to the third amino acid of another, forming 4–3 crosslinks.
source: PBPs, the targets of most β-lactams, link the fourth amino acid of one peptide side chain to the third amino acid of another, forming 4–3 crosslinks.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PBP biochemistry.

claim: L,D-transpeptidases (LDTs) link peptide side chains by the third amino acid forming 3–3 linkages.
source: Peptidoglycan crosslinks can also be catalyzed by L,D-transpeptidases (LDTs), which link peptide side chains by the third amino acid forming 3–3 linkages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about LDT biochemistry, illustrated in the figure.

claim: In mycobacteria, 3–3 crosslinks account for at least 60% of linkages.
source: In mycobacteria, these 3–3 crosslinks, are highly abundant, accounting for at least 60% of linkages (Kumar et al., 2012; Lavollay et al., 2008; Wietzerbin et al., 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are five LDTs in Mtb and six in Mycobacterium smegmatis (Msm).
source: As is the case with PBPs, there exists many copies of LDTs in the cell - there are five LDTs in Mtb and six in Mycobacterium smegmatis (Msm), a non-pathogenic relative of Mtb (Sanders et al., 2014), making genetic characterization challenging.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: LDT homologues do not appear to functionally overlap completely.
source: Also similarly to PBPs, LDT homologues do not appear to functionally overlap completely (Cordillot et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2017; Schoonmaker et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Carbapenems are β-lactam antibiotics that potently inhibit LDTs in vitro.
source: However, carbapenems, β-lactam antibiotics that potently inhibit LDTs in vitro (Cordillot et al., 2013; Dubée et al., 2012; Lavollay et al., 2008; Mainardi et al., 2007; Triboulet et al., 2013), are also effective against drug resistant Mtb in vitro and drug-sensitive Mtb in patients (Diacon et al., 2016; Hugonnet et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When Msm was incubated with FDAAs for a short 2 min pulse, incorporation was observed at both poles.
source: When we incubated Msmwith FDAAs for a short 2 min pulse ( < 2% of Msm's generation time) we observed incorporation at both poles, the sites of new PG insertion in mycobacteria (Figure 1A,B) (Aldridge et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy images in Figure 1B.

claim: A gradient of FDAA fluorescence was observed along the sidewalls, extending from the old pole and fading to a minimum at roughly mid-cell as it reaches the new pole.
source: However, we also saw a gradient of fluorescence along the sidewalls, extending from the old pole (the previously established growth pole) that fades to a minimum at roughly mid-cell as it reaches the new pole (the pole formed at the last cell division) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy images and quantification in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Three LDTs (ldtA, ldtB, ldtE) were identified from a FACS-based transposon screen as primarily responsible for FDAA incorporation.
source: From this screen, we identified three LDTs (ldtA - MSMEG_3528, ldtB - MSMEG_4745, ldtE - MSMEG_0233) (Figure 1D) that appeared primarily responsible for FDAA incorporation.
evidence: This is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Deleting ldtA, ldtB, and ldtE significantly reduced FDAA incorporation.
source: Deleting these three LDTs significantly reduced FDAA incorporation and this defect in incorporation could be partially complemented with constitutive expression of LdtE alone (ldtE-mRFP, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: FDAA incorporation and 3–3 crosslinking are both nearly abolished in ΔLDT cells.
source: FDAA incorporation and 3–3 crosslinking are both nearly abolished in ΔLDT cells and can be partially restored by complementation with a single LDT (ldtE-mRFP; ΔLDTcomp) (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplements 3B and 4).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and LC-MS/MS data in the referenced figures.

claim: FDAA incorporation in Msm is primarily LDT-dependent.
source: Thus, as might be the case in Bdellovibrio (Kuru et al., 2017), FDAA incorporation in Msm is primarily LDT-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing loss of FDAA incorporation in ΔLDT cells.

claim: A subpopulation of ΔLDT cells loses rod shape progressively over time, resulting in localized spherical blebs.
source: We observed that a subpopulation of cells loses rod shape progressively over time, resulting in localized spherical blebs (Figure 2A – top row, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures.

claim: Complemented ΔLDT cells are able to maintain rod shape.
source: Complemented cells are able to maintain rod shape (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Switching ΔLDT cells from iso- to high-osmolarity prevented bleb formation over time.
source: Indeed, switching cells from iso- to high- osmolarity prevented bleb formation over time (Figure 2A – bottom row, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy in Figure 2A.

claim: Blebs that formed in ΔLDT cells retained stain, indicating a lack of new cell wall synthesis in the region.
source: Blebs that formed in the ΔLDT cells retained stain, indicating a lack of new cell wall synthesis in the region.
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase labeling experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: WT cells maintained rod shape over time at the stained portion of the bacillus.
source: WT cells maintained rod shape over time at the stained portion of the bacillus.
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase labeling experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 3–3 crosslinks are required to counteract turgor pressure and maintain rod shape in Msm.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that 3–3 crosslinks are required to counteract turgor pressure and maintain rod shape in Msm.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the osmolarity experiments and bleb formation observations.

claim: WT cells are generally stiffer than ΔLDT cells as measured by atomic force microscopy.
source: Generally, WT cells are stiffer than ΔLDT cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Stiffness drops in the area of blebs in ΔLDT cells.
source: We found that stiffness drops in the area of blebs (Figure 2D, pink shaded).
evidence: This is supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The daughter which inherited the new pole from the previous round of division, and the oldest cell wall, consistently lost rod shape over time.
source: Indeed, the daughter which inherited the new pole from the previous round of division, and the oldest cell wall, consistently lost rod shape over time, while the old pole daughter maintained rod shape (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy tracking cell lineages in Figure 2E.

claim: Blebs localized to the oldest cell wall in ΔLDT cells.
source: In addition, blebs localized to the oldest cell wall (Figure 2B), as visualized by pulse-chase labeling of the cell wall.
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase labeling experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LDTs act locally to reinforce aging PG and to maintain rod shape in a subpopulation of Msm cells - specifically, new pole daughters.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that LDTs act locally to reinforce aging PG and to maintain rod shape in a subpopulation of Msm cells - specifically, new pole daughters (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lineage tracking and bleb localization data.

claim: Mutants of two PBPs, pbpA and ponA2, were recovered at significantly lower frequencies in ΔLDT cells compared to WT.
source: We found that mutants of two PBPs, pbpA (MSMEG_0031 c) and ponA2 (MSMEG_6201), were recovered at significantly lower frequencies in ΔLDT cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by TnSeq data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The transpeptidase (TP) activity of PonA1, which is non-essential in WT cells, becomes essential in ΔLDT cells.
source: Likewise, using allele swapping (Kieser et al., 2015b) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), a technique that tests the ability of various alleles to support viability, we found that the transpeptidase (TP) activity of PonA1, which is non-essential in WT cells (Kieser et al., 2015b), becomes essential in ΔLDT cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by allele swapping experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cells that lack 3–3 crosslinks are more dependent on 4–3 crosslinking enzymes.
source: Thus, cells that lack 3–3 crosslinks are more dependent on 4–3 crosslinking enzymes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TnSeq and allele swapping data.

claim: PonA1-RFP localization was highest at the old and new poles, where new PG is inserted.
source: We found that the distribution pattern of PonA1-RFP was highest at the old and new poles, where new PG is inserted (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—video 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: LdtE-mRFP localization is highest farther from the poles, more inward from the ends of the bacillus, at the sites of older PG.
source: Compared to PonA1-RFP, the LdtE-mRFP localization is highest farther from the poles, more inward from the ends of the bacillus (albeit in a similar gradient pattern), at the sites of older PG (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—video 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Enzymes responsible for 4–3 and 3–3 crosslinks show distinctive subcellular localizations with respect to the site of new PG synthesis.
source: Thus, enzymes responsible for 4–3 and 3–3 crosslinks show distinctive subcellular localizations with respect to the site of new PG synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the localization data of PonA1-RFP and LdtE-mRFP.

claim: DacB2 has both D,D-carboxypeptidase and D,D-endopeptidase activity on peptidoglycan substrates generated in vitro.
source: We expressed and purified DacB2 and found that it, like AmpH, had both D,D-carboxypeptidase and D,D-endopeptidase activity on peptidoglycan substrates generated in vitro (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro biochemical assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Induction of dacB2 CRISPRi knockdown led to smaller blebs in ΔLDT cells.
source: Induction of the sgRNA and dCas9 by anhydro-tetracycline (aTc) led to smaller blebs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: DacB2-mRFP localized closer to LDT-mRFP, farther from the poles, at sites of older PG.
source: Furthermore, DacB2-mRFP localized closer to LDT-mRFP, farther from the poles, at sites of older PG (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—video 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Blebs are formed in ΔLDT cells due to unchecked D,D-endopeptidase activity.
source: Taken together, these data are consistent with a model in which blebs are formed in ΔLDT cells due to unchecked D,D-endopeptidase activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the DacB2 localization and knockdown experiments.

claim: There are additional D,D-endopeptidases in M. smegmatis besides DacB2.
source: Given that bleb formation is not completely rescued by knockdown of dacB2, we speculate that there are additional D,D-endopeptidases in M. smegmatis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the incomplete rescue of the bleb phenotype.

claim: Carbapenem β-lactams target both PBPs and LDTs.
source: While Mtb can be killed by most non-carbapenem (N-C) β-lactams like amoxicillin, which largely target the PBPs, carbapenem β-lactams, which target both PBPs and LDTs (Kumar et al., 2017; Mainardi et al., 2007; Papp-Wallace et al., 2011) are also effective against Mtb (Diacon et al., 2016; Hugonnet et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The combination of amoxicillin and meropenem kills both Msm and Mtb faster than either drug alone.
source: We found that these drugs together kill both Msm and Mtb faster than either alone (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase-based killing assays shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The combination of amoxicillin and meropenem exhibits synergism in minimal inhibitory concentration in Mtb but not against Msm.
source: Furthermore, this combination exhibits synergism in minimal inhibitory concentration in Mtb but, not against Msm (where synergism is defined as Σ Fractional Inhibitory Concentration <0.5 ('Synergism Testing: Broth Microdilution Checkerboard and Broth Macrodilution Materials and methods,' 2016), Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by MIC checkerboard assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The difference in synergism between Msm and Mtb may reflect a difference in LDT expression or essentiality between the two species.
source: This may reflect a difference in LDT expression or essentiality between Msm and Mtb.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences in drug synergy.

claim: FDAA incorporation in mycobacteria shows an unusual gradient pattern.
source: We find that in mycobacteria, FDAA incorporation is primarily LDT-dependent. FDAA incorporation in Msm shows an unusual gradient pattern (Botella et al., 2017), suggesting an asymmetric distribution of tetrapeptide substrate for the LDT-dependent exchange reaction.
evidence: This is supported by the FDAA incorporation patterns observed in Figure 1 and cited prior work.

claim: Crosslinks catalyzed by LDTs are rare in model rod-shaped bacteria like E.coli and B. subtilis but are abundant in polar growing bacteria like mycobacteria, Agrobacterium tumefaciens and Sinorhizobium meliloti.
source: Crosslinks catalyzed by LDTs are rare in model rod-shaped bacteria like E.coli and B. subtilis but, are abundant in polar growing bacteria like mycobacteria, Agrobacterium tumefaciens and Sinorhizobium meliloti (Brown et al., 2012; Cameron et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2012; Lavollay et al., 2008; Pisabarro et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Msm cells lacking 3–3 crosslinks cannot maintain rod shape at sites of aging cell wall.
source: Here, we find that Msm cells lacking 3–3 crosslinks cannot maintain rod shape at sites of aging cell wall.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the bleb formation data in ΔLDT cells.

claim: 4–3 crosslinks made by PBPs appear able to maintain rod shape near the poles, the sites of newer cell wall.
source: 4–3 crosslinks made by PBPs appear able to maintain rod shape near the poles, the sites of newer cell wall (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that blebs form in older cell wall regions but not at the poles.

claim: As older cell wall moves toward the middle of the cell, it loses structural stability and begins to bleb in ΔLDT cells.
source: Over time, as older cell wall moves toward the middle of the cell, it loses structural stability, and begins to bleb.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy and pulse-chase labeling experiments.

claim: Cell wall processing must occur to de-stabilize older portions of the rod in ΔLDT cells.
source: The gradual manner in which rod shape is lost in cells lacking 3–3 crosslinks suggests that cell wall processing must occur to de-stabilize this portion of the rod.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gradual nature of bleb formation.

claim: DacB2, a D,D-endopeptidase/D,D-carboxypeptidase, localizes to sites of old cell wall.
source: Consistent with this idea, we find that an enzyme that cleaves 4–3 crosslinks, the D,D-endopeptidase/D,D-carboxypeptidase DacB2, also localizes to sites of old cell wall and knockdown of this enzyme leads to smaller blebs.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy and CRISPRi knockdown experiments.

claim: The gradient localization patterns of PonA1, LdtE and DacB2 all have local minima at mid-cell closer to the new pole.
source: Supporting this idea, we find that the gradient localization patterns of fluorescently tagged PonA1, LdtE and DacB2, (as well as FDAAs) all have local minima at mid-cell closer to the new pole- a location that correlates with the asymmetric site of division in mycobacteria (Aldridge et al., 2012; Santi et al., 2013; Eskandarian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the localization data in Figure 4 and cited prior work on division site placement.

claim: The lack of localization of PG synthesis enzymes and FDAAs at mid-cell suggests a lack of penta- and tetra- peptide substrates.
source: The lack of localization of PG synthesis enzymes and FDAAs suggests a lack of penta- and tetra- peptide substrates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the localization patterns.

claim: The region near mid-cell may be more abundantly crosslinked, as crosslinking utilizes peptide species.
source: This implies that this region of the cell may be more abundantly crosslinked, as crosslinking utilizes these peptide species.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of available peptide substrates.

claim: 3–3 crosslinking may be a signal for septal placement.
source: Could 3–3 crosslinking be a signal for septal placement?
evidence: This is speculation based on the localization patterns and lack of known septal placement mechanisms.

claim: Mycobacteria are missing known molecular septal placement mechanisms like the Noc and the Min system.
source: Mycobacteria are missing known molecular septal placement mechanisms like the Noc and the Min system (Hett and Rubin, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The major septal PG hydrolase is RipA, a D,L-endopeptidase which cleaves the bond between the second and third amino acid of PG side chains.
source: The major septal PG hydrolase is RipA, a D,L-endopeptidase which cleaves the bond between the second and third amino acid of PG side chains, a substrate available on 3–3 crosslinked material (Böth et al., 2011; Vollmer et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Atomic force microscopy revealed cell-envelope deformations formed at the pole of Msm travel to mid-cell through polar growth, marking the future site of division.
source: Transmitting information from the tip to mid-cell through polar growth was recently described in mycobacteria: atomic force microscopy revealed cell-envelope deformations formed at the pole of Msm travel to mid-cell through polar growth, marking the future site of division (Eskandarian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 3–3 crosslinks found at aging cell wall could be important for localizing cell division machinery.
source: Thus, it is intriguing to speculate that 3–3 crosslinks found at aging cell wall could be important for localizing cell division machinery.
evidence: This is speculation based on the localization patterns and division site placement.

claim: In well-studied rod-shaped bacteria like E.coli and B. subtilis, shape is maintained by MreB-directed PG synthesis along the lateral cell body.
source: In well-studied rod-shaped bacteria like E.coli and B. subtilis, shape is maintained by MreB-directed PG synthesis along the lateral cell body (Garner et al., 2011; Hussain et al., 2018; Ursell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mycobacteria maintain shape in the absence of an obvious MreB homolog, and in the absence of lateral cell wall elongation.
source: On the other hand, mycobacteria maintain shape in the absence of an obvious MreB homolog, and in the absence of lateral cell wall elongation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial cell biology.

claim: In lateral-elongating bacteria, new and old cell wall are constantly intermingled during growth.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to lateral-elongating bacteria, in which new and old cell wall are constantly intermingled during growth, polar growth segregates new and old cell wall (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about different growth modes, illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Polar growth segregates new and old cell wall in mycobacteria.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to lateral-elongating bacteria, in which new and old cell wall are constantly intermingled during growth, polar growth segregates new and old cell wall (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase labeling experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Mycobacteria appear to utilize 3–3 crosslinks at asymmetrically distributed aging cell wall to provide stability along the lateral body.
source: We find that mycobacteria appear to utilize 3–3 crosslinks at asymmetrically distributed aging cell wall to provide stability along the lateral body, something that may not be required in the presence of MreB-directed PG synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about LDT function and localization.

claim: The protein targets of two different classes of β-lactams are distributed differentially in a single cell and across the population.
source: We find that the protein targets of two different classes of β-lactams – enzymes which do very similar chemistry – PG crosslinking – are distributed differentially in a single cell and across the population.
evidence: This is supported by the localization data of PBPs and LDTs.

claim: In the absence of 3–3 crosslinks, 4–3 crosslinks become more important for cell viability.
source: In the absence of 3–3 crosslinks, 4–3 crosslinks become more important for cell viability.
evidence: This is supported by the TnSeq and allele swapping data showing increased dependence on PBPs in ΔLDT cells.

claim: A drug combination which inhibits both PBPs and LDTs will work synergistically to more quickly kill Mtb.
source: These data predict that a drug combination which inhibits both PBPs and LDTs will work synergistically to more quickly kill Mtb, a prediction we verified in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by the drug killing assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: Meropenem combined with amoxicillin/clavulanate resulted in early clearance of Mtb from patient sputum.
source: Interestingly, meropenem combined with amoxicillin/clavulanate resulted in early clearance of Mtb from patient sputum (Diacon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior clinical research.

claim: The combination of meropenem and amoxicillin might be key to accelerated killing of Mtb.
source: In fact, the combination might be key to accelerated killing of Mtb (Gonzalo and Drobniewski, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Whole genome sequencing verified all six LDT gene deletions in the ΔLDT strain.
source: Whole genome sequencing verified all six deletions and did not detect crossover events or chromosomal duplications (see supplemental methods).
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: LDTs have previously been shown to exchange non-canonical D-amino acids onto PG tetrapeptides in Vibrio cholera.
source: LDTs have previously been shown to exchange non-canonical D-amino acids onto PG tetrapeptides in Vibrio cholera (Cava et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Deletion of a subset of LDTs in Msm produces morphologic changes.
source: As deletion of a subset of LDTs in Msm produces morphologic changes (Sanders et al., 2014), we visualized ΔLDT cells by time-lapse microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: High osmolarity protects ΔLDT cells against forming blebs.
source: If the first hypothesis were true, high osmolarity should protect cells against forming blebs. Indeed, switching cells from iso- to high- osmolarity prevented bleb formation over time (Figure 2A – bottom row, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: DacB2 was identified by homology to the E. coli protein AmpH.
source: By homology to the E. coli protein AmpH, an enzyme with both D,D- carboxy- and endopeptidase activity (González-Leiza et al., 2011), we identified DacB2 (MSMEG_2433), a protein previously shown to have D,D-carboxypeptidase activity in Msm (Bansal et al., 2015), as a candidate to also harbor D,D-endopeptidase capability.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis using HHPRED and citations to prior research.

claim: DacB2 has D,D-carboxypeptidase activity in Msm.
source: By homology to the E. coli protein AmpH, an enzyme with both D,D- carboxy- and endopeptidase activity (González-Leiza et al., 2011), we identified DacB2 (MSMEG_2433), a protein previously shown to have D,D-carboxypeptidase activity in Msm (Bansal et al., 2015), as a candidate to also harbor D,D-endopeptidase capability.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Knockdown of dacB2 expression in ΔLDT cells led to smaller blebs.
source: We used a recently developed CRISPRi system for mycobacteria to knockdown dacB2 expression in ΔLDT cells (Rock et al., 2017). Induction of the sgRNA and dCas9 by anhydro-tetracycline (aTc) led to smaller blebs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPRi experiments and microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Previously published Mtb Tnseq data suggests that LDTs may be essential in the pathogen.
source: Interestingly, while we could create a strain of Msm lacking all LDTs, previously published Mtb Tnseq data suggests that LDTs may be essential in the pathogen (Kieser et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior TnSeq data.

claim: Amoxicillin and meropenem together kill both Msm and Mtb faster than either alone.
source: We found that these drugs together kill both Msm and Mtb faster than either alone (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase-based killing assays shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The combination of amoxicillin and meropenem exhibits synergism in minimal inhibitory concentration in Mtb.
source: Furthermore, this combination exhibits synergism in minimal inhibitory concentration in Mtb but, not against Msm (where synergism is defined as Σ Fractional Inhibitory Concentration <0.5 ('Synergism Testing: Broth Microdilution Checkerboard and Broth Macrodilution Materials and methods,' 2016), Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by MIC checkerboard assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The combination of amoxicillin and meropenem does not exhibit synergism in minimal inhibitory concentration in Msm.
